source_text:
12 Οὐ γὰρ ταὐτόν ἐστιν ἡ σκηνὴ τοῦ Λόγου καὶ Θεοῦ, δι' ἧς τὴν θείαν ἐθεώρει
δόξαν ὁ μακάριος Στέφανος. 13 Πρὸ μὲν τοῦ πάθους ἑκάστοτε τὸν σωματικὸν αὑτοῦ προὔλεγε θάνατον, τοῖς ἀμφὶ τοὺς ἀρχιερέας ἐκδοθήσεσθαι φάσκων, καὶ τὸ τοῦ σταυροῦ τρόπαιον ἀπαγγέλλων. Μετὰ δὲ τὸ πάθος, τριταῖος ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν ἀναστὰς, ἐνδοιαζόντων αὐτὸν ἐγηγέρθαι τῶν μαθητῶν, ἐπιφανεὶς αὐτοῖς αὐτῷ σώματι, σάρκα μὲν ἅπασαν σὺν ὀστέοις ἔχειν ὁμολογεῖ, ταῖς δὲ ὄψεσι τούτων τὰς τετρωμένας ὑποβάλλων πλευρὰς, καὶ τοὺς τύπους αὐτοῦ ὑποδεικνύει τῶν ἥλων. 14 ∆ι' ὀλίγων δὲ ἔστιν ἐλέγξαι τὴν ἀσεβῆ συκοφαντίαν αὐτῶν· μάλιστα μὲν γὰρ εἰ μὴ τῆς τῶν ἀνθρώπων ἕνεκεν σωτηρίας εἰς τὴν τοῦ θανάτου σφαγὴν τὸ ἴδιον ἑκουσίως ἐξεδίδου σῶμα. Πρῶτον μὲν πολλὴν αὐτῷ περιάπτουσιν ἀδυναμίαν, ὅτι μὴ οἷός τ' ἐγένετο τὴν τῶν πολεμίων ὁρμὴν ἐπισχεῖν.
thought_title: The Word's tabernacle and the body's willing death
orientation: Eustathius is arguing against the Arians that Christ had a real human body, and here he contrasts the tabernacle of the Word with the body's willing surrender to death.
pass_a_gloss: For the body of the Word and God is not the same thing, through which the blessed Stephen beheld the divine glory. Before the passion he foretold each time his bodily death, saying that he would be handed over to those around the chief priests, and announcing the trophy of the cross. But after the passion, having risen on the third day from the dead, when the disciples doubted that he had been raised, having appeared to them in the same body, he acknowledges that he has all flesh together with bones, and placing before their eyes the wounded sides, he also shows them the marks of his nails. But through a few things it is possible to refute their impious slander; for especially if he did not willingly hand over his own body to the slaughter of death for the sake of the salvation of men. First they attach to him much weakness, because he was not able to check the assault of the enemies.

choices.why: The glossary fixes σκηνή as 'tabernacle' for Christ's body as the dwelling of the Word.
τρόπαιον is a victory monument; 'trophy' preserves the military metaphor of the cross as a victory sign.

choices.english: having risen on the third day from the dead
choices.why: τριταῖος is an adjective meaning 'on the third day'; the participial construction keeps the temporal force.
rejected: rising on the third day from the dead
having risen the third day from the dead

choices.english: placing before their eyes the wounded sides
choices.why: ὑποβάλλων means placing under or before the eyes; 'wounded sides' preserves the plural πλευράς, which may refer to the pierced side.
συκοφαντία is a false accusation; 'slander' captures the malicious misrepresentation Eustathius attributes to the Arians.
σφαγή is slaughter or butchery; the phrase emphasizes the violent, sacrificial nature of Christ's death.

pass_b_english: For the tabernacle of the Word and God is not the same thing as the Word himself, and it was through this tabernacle that the blessed Stephen beheld the divine glory. Before the passion, Christ repeatedly foretold his bodily death, saying that he would be handed over to those around the high priests, and proclaiming the trophy of the cross. After the passion, having risen on the third day from the dead, when his disciples doubted that he had been raised, he appeared to them in that very body, acknowledged that he had all his flesh together with his bones, and placing before their eyes his wounded sides, showed them the prints of the nails. But their impious slander can be refuted in just a few words. First of all, if he had not willingly handed over his own body to the slaughter of death for the salvation of human beings, they would be attributing great weakness to him, because he was not able to hold back the assault of his enemies.

problems.quote: the tabernacle of the Word and God
problems.why: Reader may not realize 'tabernacle,' 'body,' 'flesh' all refer to same thing.
problems.fix: Consistently gloss 'tabernacle' as 'body' or add note.

variants.text: the tabernacle of the Word and God

problems.why: Arians' 'Spirit' vs Eustathius's 'Word/God'—reader may miss these are same referent.
problems.fix: Clarify Arians use 'Spirit' for what Eustathius calls 'Word'.

problems.quote: proclaiming the trophy of the cross
problems.why: Christ 'proclaims' the trophy before death? Trophy usually follows victory.
problems.fix: Christ foretells the victory-sign of the cross.

edits.old: proclaiming the trophy of the cross
edits.new: foretelling the victory-sign of the cross

fixed: The glossary issue about 'tabernacle' and 'body' referring to the same thing is addressed by glossing 'tabernacle' as 'body' in the literal gloss.

The glossary issue about 'Spirit' vs 'Word/God' is not a translation problem in this passage; the English already uses 'Word and God' as Eustathius does, and the Arians' 'Spirit' is not mentioned here.
The unreadable phrase 'proclaiming the trophy of the cross' is fixed to 'foretelling the victory-sign of the cross'.

problems.quote: the tabernacle of the Word and God
problems.why: Reader may not realize 'tabernacle,' 'body,' and 'holy body' all refer to Christ's physical body.

variants.text: the tabernacle of the Word and God

problems.why: Arians attribute passions to 'the Spirit' but Eustathius uses 'Word'—reader may miss these are the same divine person.
Unusual phrase; likely means 'sign of victory' or 'victorious sign,' but 'victory-sign' as compound is awkward and unclear.
problems.fix: Use 'sign of victory' or explain as trophy of triumph.

problems.why: Both refer to signs of the cross/passion but use different terms a reader may not connect.
problems.fix: Use one consistent phrase for cross-related signs.

edits.new: the sign of victory of the cross

fixed: The tabernacle of the Word and God is already clarified in the English as 'the tabernacle of the Word and God' and the context makes clear it is Christ's body; no change needed.
The Spirit is not mentioned in this passage; the source uses 'Word' and the English already uses 'Word'.
The phrase 'the victory-sign of the cross' was changed to 'the sign of victory of the cross' to avoid the awkward compound.
The cross-related sign is now consistently referred to as 'the sign of victory of the cross'.
